implementation_notes: Rails ships both halves of the pattern in two modules rather than one object: ActiveRecord::Base.transaction (also available per model instance) opens a real transaction on that model's connection and rolls back when an exception escapes, while ActiveModel::Dirty tracks per-attribute changes (changed?, changes, name_was) that ActiveRecord applies on save - and save/destroy are themselves wrapped in a transaction. So the transaction block is the boundary, dirty tracking is the register, and save is the flush. Sequel takes the boundary-only route: DB.transaction with after_commit/after_rollback hooks, savepoints via savepoint: true or auto_savepoint: true, prepared transactions, and explicit dataset writes - no dirty tracking, so a flush step must be written by hand.
code_sketch:
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do          # boundary; rollback on raise
  customer = Customer.find(id)
  customer.name = "new"                    # ActiveModel::Dirty records it
  customer.changed?                        # => true
  customer.save!                           # flush: UPDATE ... WHERE id =
  Audit.create!(customer_id: id, field: "name")
end                                        # COMMIT; after_commit callbacks fire
pitfalls: A transaction acts on one database connection, so models on different databases are not protected together - the documented workaround of nesting transactions per class is a poor substitute for distributed transactions.
Rescuing ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid inside the block leaves the transaction unusable on PostgreSQL, so the error must escape the block.
Nested transaction calls reuse the parent by default; requires_new: true is needed for a real savepoint, and a nested ActiveRecord::Rollback is swallowed by the parent block.
Instance attributes are not reverted by a rollback, and external side effects belong in after_commit, not inside the block.

variants.name: Sequel DB.transaction with explicit dataset writes
variants.implementation_notes: Sequel is autocommit by default, so the unit of work is an explicit DB.transaction block containing the dataset writes (a few operations such as Model#save are wrapped implicitly). It provides savepoints (savepoint: true), transaction hooks (after_commit/after_rollback), isolation levels and automatic retry on serialization failures, but no dirty tracking: the change set is whatever the block writes. Prefer it over ActiveRecord when the application is statement-oriented and wants the boundary without the ORM's tracking machinery.
variants.code_sketch:
DB.transaction(isolation: :serializable, retry_on: [Sequel::SerializationFailure]) do
  DB[:customers].where(id: id).update(name: name)
  DB[:audits].insert(customer_id: id, field: 'name')
  DB.after_commit { cache.delete("customer:#{id}") }
end   # COMMIT; Sequel::Rollback or any exception rolls back
pitfalls: Automatic retry re-runs the whole block, so it must only be used with idempotent work; logging and external calls inside the block will repeat.
Nested transaction calls reuse the existing transaction unless savepoint: true is passed, so an inner failure can roll back the outer work.
